subject: Cloud Computing
title: Availability Zones and Regions
description: A fast breakdown of Availability Zones and Regions for builders.

hook.text: AWS has data centers in 33 countries. But they're not randomly scattered — they're carefully layered.

buildup.text: A region is a geographic area like 'US East' or 'Europe West.' Each contains multiple availability zones.

discovery.text: Each zone is a separate data center with its own power, cooling, and networking. Independent failure.

twist.text: Most outages hit one zone, not the whole region. Spreading across zones keeps your app running.

climax.text: Multi-region deployments survive even regional disasters. But they're complex and expensive to build.

punchline.text: One zone can fail. If you planned right, nobody notices.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of availability zones within a cloud region?
options: To provide independent infrastructure so one zone's failure doesn't affect others
To group servers by programming language compatibility
To separate free-tier and paid customers into different areas

details.summary: Cloud regions are geographic areas containing multiple availability zones, which are physically separate data center facilities with independent power, cooling, and networking. Deploying across multiple AZs protects against facility-level failures while keeping latency under two milliseconds.
details.whyItMatters: Multi-AZ deployment is the most fundamental cloud resilience pattern. Understanding regions and AZs is essential for designing applications that survive infrastructure failures.
takeaways: Regions are geographic areas, AZs are separate facilities within them
AZs have independent power, cooling, and networking
Latency between AZs in a region is typically under 2 milliseconds

faq.question: How many AZs should you use?
faq.answer: Deploy across at least two AZs for high availability. Three AZs provide additional resilience and are recommended for production workloads. Each AZ should be able to handle the full application load independently so that losing one AZ causes no user-visible impact.

faq.question: How do you choose a cloud region?
faq.answer: Consider proximity to users for low latency, data sovereignty requirements, available services, and pricing which varies by region. Some services are only available in specific regions. Cost-sensitive workloads can benefit from less popular regions with lower pricing.
